metadata.title: Sinc² to Golden Rule — Does the Viz Show the Physics?
metadata.purpose: Critique the sinc²(δT/2)→δ(δ) Fermi's Golden Rule D3 viz from quantum-mechanics-vol3

beats.narration_text: Bonjour. Liam, in for Bear. Someone asked Claude to visualize how the sinc-squared function converges to a Dirac delta as interaction time grows — the kernel step inside Fermi's Golden Rule. We are judging the visualization, not the physics.

props.command: Hey Claude, write me a visualization for the sinc-squared to delta-function limit in Fermi's Golden Rule.

beats.narration_text: Three sinc-squared curves on a log y-axis: T equals 1 in black, 10 in gray, 100 in red. A dashed fourth curve tracks the T-slider, currently at 5. The x-axis runs from negative four-pi to positive four-pi in detuning delta. Top-right: a log-log panel shows peak height and area versus T, with slope annotations. Below it, a physics console verifying three numerical ratios. Bottom-right: a linear plot of the area integral two-pi-T against T.
beats.new_visual_element: SOURCE-CUT media/output.mp4 — baseline hold, T-slider at 5

beats.narration_text: The T slider drives T from 1 to 100. The function is T-squared times sinc-squared of delta-T over 2. As T grows, the peak rises as T-squared, the half-width shrinks as 1 over T, and the area scales linearly as 2-pi-T. The viewer's prediction question: where does this sequence go? A function with growing peak, shrinking width, and constant area-per-T — converging to a Dirac delta.

Three wins. First, the log scale is the right encoding here. Without it, T equals 100 obliterates T equals 1 and 10 — four orders of magnitude in peak height on a single chart. Log scale makes all three coexist and readable. Second, the physics console is genuine: three self-checking ratios computed live — peak ratio 100, width ratio 0.1, area ratio 10. The student can verify the equations are honest, not just trusted. Third, the log-log scaling panel: slope-2 for peak, slope-1 for area, labeled and drawn in the data itself. That is the power law argument made visible, not stated.
beats.new_visual_element: Freeze: media/B03.png — default view, all three reference curves visible on log axis

beats.narration_text: Two problems. First, the critical one: the x-axis is fixed at plus-or-minus four-pi, calibrated to T equals 1. At T equals 100, the first zero of sinc-squared lands at delta equals 2-pi over 100 — 0.06, which is one-half percent of the axis width. The peak you are supposed to see sharpening into a delta function is physically invisible — a single-pixel red line. The fix: zoom the x-axis with T. Show delta from minus-10 over T to plus-10 over T so the peak always fills the frame and the convergence becomes an animation the student can watch. Second: the top-right panel y-axis is labeled only 'value' — uninformative for a panel whose entire purpose is to show two distinct power-law scalings.
beats.new_visual_element: Freeze: media/B04.png — T-slider at 100, dashed curve invisible inside fixed T=100 curve

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Log scale and live physics checks earn this visualization real classroom time — but the fixed x-axis hides the one thing it's supposed to show: the delta function limit becoming visible. Fix the x-axis zoom first, then deploy.

artifactLines: Log y-scale: correct — lets T=1, 10, 100 coexist across 4 orders of magnitude
Physics console: self-checking ratios, genuine verification
Fixed x-axis at ±4π hides the delta-function convergence entirely
Area panel annotation reverses the causal logic of the limit
Fix: zoom x as ±10/T so the sharpening is visible before deploying

beats.narration_text: I have a D3 visualization of the sinc-squared of delta-T over 2 converging to a Dirac delta — Fermi's Golden Rule. The x-axis is fixed at plus or minus four-pi. At T equals 100, the peak sharpens to a single pixel and the convergence is invisible. Rewrite the x-axis domain to zoom with T: show delta from minus 10 over T to plus 10 over T, so the peak always fills roughly half the plot width. Keep all four curves — T equals 1, 10, and 100 as fixed references, and the slider curve — but clip them to the zoomed window. Add a small annotation showing the first zero location at 2-pi over T. Keep the physics console and the log-linear toggle unchanged.
